chapters.title: Reading the land and its people

points.title: Contour lines
points.brief: Contour lines join places of the same height on a topographic map. Lines close together show steep land, and lines far apart show gentle slopes.

points.title: Drawing a cross-section
points.brief: A cross-section shows the shape of the land along a line on a map, drawn by marking where each contour crosses the line and plotting its height.

points.title: Aerial and satellite images
points.brief: Photos from above show land use, landforms and how places change over time, which a map may not show.

points.title: Population density
points.brief: Population density is the number of people per square kilometre. Shading areas on a map by density shows where people crowd together and where few live.

chapters.title: Landscapes of Australia and the world

points.title: Landscapes and landforms
points.brief: A landscape is a large area with its own look, made of many landforms. A landform is a single feature such as a mountain, valley, dune or headland.

points.title: Types of landscape
points.brief: The world's main landscapes include mountains, deserts, grasslands, forests, wetlands and coasts, each shaped by climate and the rocks beneath.

points.title: Australia's distinctive landscapes
points.brief: Australia is mostly flat and dry, with deserts in the centre, the Great Dividing Range in the east, tropical rainforests in the north and long coasts, and famous landforms such as Uluru.

points.title: Plate tectonics and mountain building
points.brief: The Earth's crust is broken into plates that move. Where they push together, rock is forced up into mountains such as the Himalayas.

points.title: Folding and faulting
points.brief: Folding bends layers of rock into waves when they are squeezed. Faulting cracks rock so that blocks move up, down or sideways.

points.title: Volcanism
points.brief: Volcanoes form where melted rock rises through the crust and erupts as lava, ash and gas, building new landforms such as cones and plateaus.

points.title: Physical and chemical weathering
points.brief: Weathering breaks rock down where it sits. Physical weathering cracks it, such as by frost or heating and cooling, and chemical weathering changes it, such as by rusting or dissolving.

points.title: Erosion, transportation and deposition
points.brief: Water, wind, waves and ice wear rock away, carry the pieces and drop them elsewhere, building beaches and dunes and carving cliffs and stacks such as the Twelve Apostles.

points.title: Rock types and landforms
points.brief: Igneous rock forms from cooled magma, sedimentary rock from layers of sediment, and metamorphic rock from heat and pressure. Harder rocks resist erosion and stand out.

points.title: Country and landforms
points.brief: For First Nations Australians, landforms are part of Country/Place. Aboriginal Dreaming and Torres Strait Islander Creation stories explain how the land was made and carry law and knowledge.

points.title: Landforms with special significance
points.brief: Uluru is sacred to the Anangu, and Budj Bim in Gunditjmara Country holds ancient eel traps. Such places have names, stories and meanings for their Traditional Owners.

points.title: Landscapes, beauty and tourism
points.brief: People value landscapes for their beauty and spiritual meaning, such as Mount Fuji in Japan, and many draw tourists, which brings money and pressure.

points.title: Land clearing and erosion
points.brief: Clearing forests for farms or palm oil, and overused walking tracks, strip the ground cover, so soil erodes and washes into rivers.

points.title: Mining and urban development
points.brief: Mines, quarries and new suburbs remove landforms and vegetation and can pollute water and air around them.

points.title: River regulation
points.brief: Dams, weirs and straightened channels control river flow for water supply and flood control, but change the floods that wetlands and fish need, as on the Murray-Darling.

points.title: First Nations knowledge in managing landscapes
points.brief: Places such as Kakadu and Uluru-Kata Tjuta are jointly managed with Traditional Owners, whose knowledge of fire, plants and animals guides how the land is cared for.

points.title: Earthquakes
points.brief: Earthquakes happen when stress builds along a fault and the rock suddenly slips, sending shaking waves through the ground.

points.title: Volcanic eruptions as hazards
points.brief: Eruptions threaten people with lava flows, falling ash, poisonous gases and fast flows of hot ash and rock.

points.title: Tsunamis
points.brief: A tsunami is a series of huge waves, usually set off by an undersea earthquake, that floods coasts far from where it started.

points.title: Landslides and avalanches
points.brief: Landslides happen when soil and rock slide down a slope, often after heavy rain or land clearing. Avalanches are masses of snow sliding down a mountain.

points.title: Reducing a geomorphological hazard's impact
points.brief: Stronger buildings, warning systems, evacuation plans and keeping homes off unstable land cut the harm. Poorer places often suffer more because they have fewer of these.

points.title: Urban growth and urbanisation
points.brief: Urban growth is cities getting bigger. Urbanisation is a rising share of a country's people living in cities rather than the country.

points.title: Push and pull factors
points.brief: Push factors drive people away from a place, such as no jobs or drought. Pull factors draw them to a place, such as work, schools and services.

points.title: Megacities and urban corridors
points.brief: A megacity has over 10 million people, such as Los Angeles with its surrounds. An urban corridor is a chain of cities joined together, such as Boston to Washington.

points.title: Economic change and cities
points.brief: When industries grow or close, cities change. Old industrial areas can decline or be rebuilt as new housing and offices, called urban renewal.

points.title: Environmental effects of cities
points.brief: Growing cities use more water and energy and make more waste and emissions, but dense cities can also share services more efficiently.

points.title: Urban concentration in Australia
points.brief: Most Australians live in a few large coastal capital cities, so Australia is one of the most urbanised countries in the world.

points.title: Causes of Australia's urban concentration
points.brief: European settlement began at ports, each colony grew around its capital, exports left from those ports, and the dry inland supports few people.

points.title: Comparing Australia and the United States
points.brief: The United States has many large cities spread across the country, while Australia's are few and mostly on the coast.

points.title: Density and distance from the city centre
points.brief: Population density is usually highest near the central business district and falls toward the rural-urban fringe.

points.title: Planning for population growth
points.brief: Governments plan for growing cities with new housing, transport, services and green space, aiming to keep them sustainable and liveable.

points.title: Decentralisation
points.brief: Decentralisation spreads people and jobs away from the biggest cities to regional centres. Canberra was planned partly with this aim.

points.title: Internal and international migration
points.brief: Internal migration is moving within a country. International migration is moving from one country to another.

points.title: Types of migration
points.brief: Migration can be permanent, temporary for work or study, circular back and forth, or forced, as for refugees escaping war or persecution.

points.title: Mining and internal migration
points.brief: Mining booms draw workers to regions such as the Pilbara and the Bowen Basin, often as fly-in fly-out workers who live elsewhere.

points.title: Internal migration in China
points.brief: Hundreds of millions of people in China have moved from farms to coastal cities for factory work, growing the cities and leaving older people and children in villages.

points.title: Migration and cultural diversity
points.brief: International migration has made Australia's cities culturally diverse, with migrants mostly settling in the large capitals.
